imo-isl-2013-a1.prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}$ be arbitrary real numbers. Define the sequences $u_0,\dots,u_n$ and $v_0,\dots,v_n$ inductively by $u_0=u_1=v_0=v_1=1$, and
$$u_{k+1}=u_k+a_ku_{k-1},\qquad v_{k+1}=v_k+a_{n-k}v_{k-1}\qquad\text{for }k=1,\dots,n-1.$$
Prove that $u_n=v_n$.
imo-isl-2013-a1.answer: $u_k=\sum_I\prod_{i\in I}a_i$ over all sets $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,k-1\}$ with no two consecutive elements; $v_n$ is the same sum with $a_i$ replaced by $a_{n-i}$, and $i\mapsto n-i$ permutes these sets.

imo-isl-2013-a2.prompt:
Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a>b$ and $c>d$ with $a\ne c$ or $b\ne d$, such that
$$\left|\frac{a-b}{c-d}-1\right|<\frac{1}{100000}.$$
imo-isl-2013-a2.answer: Sort all $\binom{2000}{2}$ differences $D_1\le\dots\le D_m$. If no ratio $D_{i+1}/D_i$ is below $1+10^{-5}$, then $D_m/D_1\ge(1+10^{-5})^{m-1}>2\cdot10^5$, and the closest pair $x<y$ together with the extreme element $z$ far from $x$ gives $\left|\frac{z-y}{z-x}-1\right|=\frac{y-x}{|z-x|}<10^{-5}$ (or the analogous pair on the left).

imo-isl-2013-a4.prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer, and consider a sequence $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ of positive integers. Extend it periodically to an infinite sequence $a_1,a_2,\dots$ by defining $a_{n+i}=a_i$ for all $i\ge1$. If
$$a_1\le a_2\le\dots\le a_n\le a_1+n$$
and
$$a_{a_i}\le n+i-1\qquad\text{for }i=1,2,\dots,n,$$
prove that
$$a_1+\dots+a_n\le n^2.$$
imo-isl-2013-a4.answer: First $a_i\le n+i-1$ for all $i$, so $a_1\le n$. If $a_t\le n<a_{t+1}$, then $a_1\le t$, all $a_j\le n+t$, and with $b_i=\#\{j>t: a_j\ge n+i\}$ one has $\sum_{j>t}a_j=n(n-t)+\sum_{i\le t}b_i$ and $a_i+b_i\le n$ for $i\le t$.

imo-isl-2013-a5.prompt:
Let $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ be the set of all nonnegative integers. Find all the functions $f:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ satisfying the relation
$$f(f(f(n)))=f(n+1)+1$$
for all $n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$.
imo-isl-2013-a5.answer: Two functions: $f(n)=n+1$ for all $n$; and $f(n)=n+1$ if $n\equiv0,2\pmod4$, $f(n)=n+5$ if $n\equiv1\pmod4$, $f(n)=n-3$ if $n\equiv3\pmod4$.

imo-isl-2013-a6.prompt:
Let $m\ne0$ be an integer. Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with real coefficients such that
$$(x^3-mx^2+1)P(x+1)+(x^3+mx^2+1)P(x-1)=2(x^3-mx+1)P(x)$$
for all real numbers $x$.

imo-isl-2013-c1.prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find the smallest integer $k$ with the following property: Given any real numbers $a_1,\dots,a_d$ such that $a_1+a_2+\dots+a_d=n$ and $0\le a_i\le1$ for $i=1,2,\dots,d$, it is possible to partition these numbers into $k$ groups (some of which may be empty) such that the sum of the numbers in each group is at most $1$.

imo-isl-2013-c3.prompt:
A crazy physicist discovered a new kind of particle which he called an imon, after some of them mysteriously appeared in his lab. Some pairs of imons in the lab can be entangled, and each imon can participate in many entanglement relations. The physicist has found a way to perform the following two kinds of operations with these particles, one operation at a time.

(i) If some imon is entangled with an odd number of other imons in the lab, then the physicist can destroy it.

(ii) At any moment, he may double the whole family of imons in his lab by creating a copy $I'$ of each imon $I$. During this procedure, the two copies $I'$ and $J'$ become entangled if and only if the original imons $I$ and $J$ are entangled, and each copy $I'$ becomes entangled with its original imon $I$; no other entanglements occur or disappear at this moment.

Prove that the physicist may apply a sequence of such operations resulting in a family of imons, no two of which are entangled.
imo-isl-2013-c3.answer: In graph language: if the graph has a proper colouring with $n>1$ colours, delete odd-degree vertices until all degrees are even, double (now all degrees are odd; colour $I'$ with the colour of $I$ plus one, cyclically), and delete the independent colour class $n$ vertex by vertex. This reduces the number of colours; repeat until one colour, i.e. no edges, remains.

imo-isl-2013-c4.prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $A$ be a subset of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. An $A$-partition of $n$ into $k$ parts is a representation of $n$ as a sum $n=a_1+\dots+a_k$, where the parts $a_1,\dots,a_k$ belong to $A$ and are not necessarily distinct. The number of different parts in such a partition is the number of (distinct) elements in the set $\{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k\}$.

We say that an $A$-partition of $n$ into $k$ parts is optimal if there is no $A$-partition of $n$ into $r$ parts with $r<k$. Prove that any optimal $A$-partition of $n$ contains at most $\sqrt[3]{6n}$ different parts.
imo-isl-2013-c4.answer: If the distinct parts are $b_1<\dots<b_s$ with $s^3>6n$: for each $k$ there are $k(s-k)+1$ different sums of $k$-element subsets, $\frac{s(s^2+5)}6>n$ values in $[1,n]$ in total, so two subsets $X,Y$ of different sizes $|X|<|Y|$ have equal sums; replacing the parts in $Y$ by those in $X$ gives a partition with fewer parts.

imo-isl-2013-c5.prompt:
Let $r$ be a positive integer, and let $a_0,a_1,\dots$ be an infinite sequence of real numbers. Assume that for all nonnegative integers $m$ and $s$ there exists a positive integer $n\in[m+1,m+r]$ such that
$$a_m+a_{m+1}+\dots+a_{m+s}=a_n+a_{n+1}+\dots+a_{n+s}.$$
Prove that the sequence is periodic, i.e. there exists some $p\ge1$ such that $a_{n+p}=a_n$ for all $n\ge0$.
imo-isl-2013-c5.answer: With $s=0$ the sequence takes at most $r$ values, so some $p\le r^r$ satisfies $A_d=A_{d+p}$ for infinitely many $d$, where $A_d=(a_d,\dots,a_{d+r-1})$. Using the condition for sums of $p$ consecutive terms one shows $A_{d+1}=A_{d+1+p}\Rightarrow A_d=A_{d+p}$, hence $a_{d+p}=a_d$ for all $d$.

imo-isl-2013-c6.prompt: In some country several pairs of cities are connected by direct two-way flights. It is possible to go from any city to any other by a sequence of flights. The distance between two cities is defined to be the least possible number of flights required to go from one of them to the other. It is known that for any city there are at most $100$ cities at distance exactly three from it. Prove that there is no city such that more than $2550$ other cities have distance exactly four from it.
imo-isl-2013-c6.answer: Take a minimal set $A^*$ of neighbours of $x$ such that every city at distance 4 from $x$ is at distance 3 from some member of $A^*$; $|A^*|=m$. As $m(101-m)\le2550$, some $a\in A^*$ has at least $102-m$ such cities at distance 3, leaving at most $m-2$ other cities at distance 3 from $a$; but every $y\in A^*\setminus\{a\}$ yields a different city at distance 3 from $a$ and at most 3 from $x$.

imo-isl-2013-c8.prompt:
Players $A$ and $B$ play a paintful game on the real line. Player $A$ has a pot of paint with four units of black ink. A quantity $p$ of this ink suffices to blacken a (closed) real interval of length $p$. In every round, player $A$ picks some positive integer $m$ and provides $1/2^m$ units of ink from the pot. Player $B$ then picks an integer $k$ and blackens the interval from $k/2^m$ to $(k+1)/2^m$ (some parts of this interval may have been blackened before). The goal of player $A$ is to reach a situation where the pot is empty and the interval $[0,1]$ is not completely blackened.

Decide whether there exists a strategy for player $A$ to win in a finite number of moves.
acceptedAnswers: No, there is no such strategy

imo-isl-2013-g2.prompt: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of a triangle $ABC$. Denote by $M$ and $N$ the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, and denote by $T$ the midpoint of the arc $BC$ of $\omega$ not containing $A$. The circumcircles of the triangles $AMT$ and $ANT$ intersect the perpendicular bisectors of $AC$ and $AB$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively; assume that $X$ and $Y$ lie inside the triangle $ABC$. The lines $MN$ and $XY$ intersect at $K$. Prove that $KA=KT$.
imo-isl-2013-g2.answer: The reflection in the perpendicular bisector $\ell$ of $AT$ maps $M\mapsto X$ and $N\mapsto Y$ (it preserves circle $AMT$ and maps line $OM$ to line $ON$), so it swaps the lines $MN$ and $XY$ and fixes their intersection $K$; hence $K\in\ell$.

imo-isl-2013-g3.prompt:
In a triangle $ABC$, let $D$ and $E$ be the feet of the angle bisectors of angles $A$ and $B$, respectively. A rhombus is inscribed into the quadrilateral $AEDB$ (all vertices of the rhombus lie on different sides of $AEDB$). Let $\varphi$ be the non-obtuse angle of the rhombus. Prove that
$$\varphi\le\max\{\angle BAC,\angle ABC\}.$$
imo-isl-2013-g3.answer: For points $L$ on $DE$, $d(L,AC)+d(L,BC)=d(L,AB)$ (true at $D$ and $E$, and affine). For the rhombus $KLMN$ ($K\in AE$, $L\in ED$, $M\in DB$, $N\in BA$) this reads $\sin\mu+\sin\nu=\sin\delta+\sin\varepsilon$ for the angles its sides make with the sides of the triangle; if its angle at $K$ exceeded $\max(\angle A,\angle B)$, then $\mu<\delta<90^\circ$ and $\nu<\varepsilon<90^\circ$, a contradiction.

imo-isl-2013-g4.prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B>\angle C$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be two different points on line $AC$ such that $\angle PBA=\angle QBA=\angle ACB$ and $A$ is located between $P$ and $C$. Suppose that there exists an interior point $D$ of segment $BQ$ for which $PD=PB$. Let the ray $AD$ intersect the circle $ABC$ at $R\ne A$. Prove that $QB=QR$.
imo-isl-2013-g4.answer: $PB$ is tangent to the circumcircle, so $PD^2=PB^2=PA\cdot PC$ and $\triangle PAD\sim\triangle PDC$, giving $\angle ADP=\angle DCA$. From $\triangle AQB\sim\triangle ABC$, $\angle AQB=\angle ABC=\angle ARC$, so $D,R,C,Q$ are concyclic and $\angle DRQ=\angle DCQ=\angle ADP$. Then $\angle QBR=\angle ADB-\angle ARB=\angle ADP+2\gamma-\gamma=\angle DRQ+\gamma=\angle QRB$.

imo-isl-2013-g5.prompt: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with $AB=DE$, $BC=EF$, $CD=FA$, and $\angle A-\angle D=\angle C-\angle F=\angle E-\angle B$. Prove that the diagonals $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ are concurrent.
imo-isl-2013-g5.answer: In complex numbers, $\overrightarrow{DE}=r\,\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{FA}=r\,\overrightarrow{CD}$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=r\,\overrightarrow{EF}$ for a single unimodular $r$. Summing the sides gives $(1+r)(\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{CD}+\overrightarrow{EF})=0$: either the hexagon is centrally symmetric, or the three vectors sum to zero, and then a direct computation shows that a point of line $AD$ lies on $BE$ iff it lies on $CF$.

imo-isl-2013-n1.prompt:
Let $\mathbb Z_{>0}$ be the set of positive integers. Find all functions $f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}$ such that
$$m^2+f(n)\mid mf(m)+n$$
for all positive integers $m$ and $n$.
imo-isl-2013-n1.answer: Only $f(n)=n$ ($m=n=2$ gives $f(2)=2$; then $m=2$ gives $f(n)\le n$ and $m=n$ gives $f(n)\ge n$).

imo-isl-2013-n3.prompt: Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that the largest prime divisor of $n^4+n^2+1$ is equal to the largest prime divisor of $(n+1)^4+(n+1)^2+1$.
imo-isl-2013-n3.answer: With $q_n$ the largest prime factor of $n^2+n+1$: $n^4+n^2+1=(n^2-n+1)(n^2+n+1)$ gives $p_n=\max(q_{n-1},q_n)$ with $q_{n-1}\ne q_n$, so every local maximum $q_{n-1}<q_n>q_{n+1}$ gives $p_n=p_{n+1}$; there are infinitely many local maxima because $q$ can neither decrease forever nor increase forever ($q_{(k+1)^2}=\max(q_k,q_{k+1})$).

imo-isl-2013-n4.prompt: Determine whether there exists an infinite sequence of nonzero digits $a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots$ and a positive integer $N$ such that for every integer $k>N$, the number $\overline{a_ka_{k-1}\dots a_1}$ is a perfect square.

imo-isl-2013-n5.prompt:
Fix an integer $k\ge2$. Two players, called Ana and Banana, play the following game of numbers: Initially, some integer $n\ge k$ gets written on the blackboard. Then they take moves in turn, with Ana beginning. A player making a move erases the number $m$ just written on the blackboard and replaces it by some number $m'$ with $k\le m'<m$ that is coprime to $m$. The first player who cannot move anymore loses.

An integer $n\ge k$ is called *good* if Banana has a winning strategy when the initial number is $n$, and *bad* otherwise.

Consider two integers $n,n'\ge k$ with the property that each prime number $p\le k$ divides $n$ if and only if it divides $n'$. Prove that either both $n$ and $n'$ are good or both are bad.
imo-isl-2013-n5.answer: $n$ is good iff every move from $n$ leads to a bad number, so two good numbers are never coprime; as $k$ is good, every good number has a prime factor $\le k$. Any $b\ge k$ with a small prime factor can be replaced by a number $x$ with $k\le x\le b$, the same small primes and no big ones. Then a minimal counterexample $(a,b)$, $a$ bad, $b$ good, with $a\to r$ a move to a good $r$, leads to a small prime dividing both $a$ and $r$.

imo-isl-2013-n6.answer: The constant functions $f\equiv C$ ($C\in\mathbb Z$), the floor function $f(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor$, and the ceiling function $f(x)=\lceil x\rceil$.
